explain.say: An LCD screen does not make its own light. White LEDs behind it shine all the time, and millions of tiny shutters in front decide how much of that light gets through each dot.

explain.say: Light passes a polarising filter, then a thin layer of liquid crystal. With no voltage, the crystal twists the light so it fits through the front polariser; a voltage untwists it, and the front filter blocks it.

explain.say: A thin-film transistor behind every subpixel acts as its switch, and the screen updates them row by row many times a second. Because the shutters always leak a little, LCD blacks look slightly grey.

faq.a: Light waves wiggle in all directions. A polariser is a filter that only lets through waves wiggling in one direction. An LCD has two, crossed, so light only gets through if the liquid crystal turns it in between.

faq.q: What does the liquid crystal do?
faq.a: Liquid crystal molecules flow like a liquid but line up like a crystal. In a screen they twist the direction of the light passing through; a voltage makes them straighten, which changes how much light the front polariser lets out.
asks: How does liquid crystal block light?

faq.q: How does an LCD make colours?
faq.a: Each pixel has red, green and blue subpixels with coloured filters. By letting different amounts of light through each, the screen mixes any colour: all three fully open looks white, all closed looks black.

TFT means thin-film transistor. Every subpixel has its own tiny transistor printed on the glass, acting as a switch that sets and holds its voltage until the next refresh. Almost all LCD screens today are TFT screens.

faq.q: Why can't an LCD show true black?
faq.a: The backlight stays on behind the whole screen, and the liquid crystal shutters cannot block light perfectly, so a little always leaks through. Some screens dim zones of the backlight to help.
asks: Why does my screen glow in the dark when showing black?

facts: A 1920 by 1080 screen has about 2 million pixels and over 6 million subpixels.
